You said on the phone you want to put this to Milan on Tuesday. Read me the first line you plan to use.
"I wish we had known about the reserving gap in June."
Good. That line puts the date on the record and leaves nobody to defend. Now tell me what you had written before you rewrote it.
"We were told too late." Same fact, same date, and it arrives with a defendant attached.
It does. And what about the version I am afraid you will reach for on Tuesday, twenty minutes in, when somebody glosses over it again?
"I wish they would tell us earlier." I know. That one is about their behaviour, not about June, and it will be repeated to them in those exact words.
It will, and without your face on it. So say the regret once, tell them it is not a grievance, and then ask for what?
A standing item on the monthly call, with an owner here and an owner in Milan. If we hear it early, we course-correct while the correction is still small.
Then you do not need the second wish at all. Ask for the line on the agenda, and let the regret do the quiet work.
That is not a grievance, and nobody here needs to explain it.

What I am asking for is a standing item on the monthly call.

There is a sentence English gives you that other languages do not hand over so easily. I wish we had known in June. Say it slowly and notice what it does not contain. There is no subject who failed. There is no verb of accusation. And yet everybody in the room understands exactly what happened, and when. That is not softness, it is precision without a defendant. The moment you say you told us too late, two things happen. The other side stops listening to the content and starts defending the person, and your own credibility narrows to the size of the grievance. I have watched very capable directors lose a year of influence in one sentence. So use the wish for facts about the past. Use it once, keep it short, and follow it immediately with what you are asking for. A regret with no request is just a complaint in a good suit.

There is one form of the wish I use carefully now, and I learned that the hard way. I wish they would tell us earlier is not a regret about the past. It is a judgement on how people behave now, and everyone hears it that way, including the people upstairs. In a group where the head office sits in another country, that sentence travels further than you intended and it arrives without your tone attached. So I made myself a rule. If the thing I want is a fact on the record, I use I wish we had known. If the thing I want is a change in behaviour, I do not use the wish at all. I ask for a mechanism instead: a standing item, an owner, a date. Nobody can take offence at a line on an agenda, and the agenda outlives whoever is annoyed with whom this month.
